articles.desc: Any single ecosystem will provide many ecosystem functions. In this study, we assessed the impact of climate, landscape and biotic community on ecosystem functioning in the temperate and tropical zone, with potential trade‐offs among ecosystem functions in both zones. To this aim, we measured a diverse set of insect‐related functions – including herbivory, seed dispersal, predation, decomposition and pollination – at 50 sites across Madagascar and 171 sites across Sweden, while characterizing the insect community at each site. For the temperate zone, we found that abiotic factors were most important in driving ecosystem functioning, while in the tropical zone, effects of biotic drivers were most pronounced. In the temperate zone, most functions were uncorrelated, but in the tropical zone, most ecosystem functions increased in concert. Our study suggests that the functioning of temperate and tropical ecosystems differs fundamentally in terms of patterns and drivers. articles.title: Global patterns of cultivated plant diversity and their implications for invasion
articles.desc: People have cultivated plants for their wide-ranging services for millennia, introducing thousands of species to new regions through human migration and trade. This suggests that global regional patterns of naturalization are most directly shaped by the human-mediated introduction of plants for cultivation. Our findings provide a broad description of cultivated plant diversity and demonstrate the tight coupling of cultivation and naturalization at the global scale.

articles.desc: Heatwaves are increasing in intensity, frequency, and duration and may drive the responses of organisms to climate change more strongly than gradual increases in mean temperature. The effects of heatwave events on wildlife remain poorly understood because the magnitude of these effects often depends on environmental the context: additional environmental stressors can exacerbate the impact of extreme temperatures. Here, we test whether the impact of extreme heat on adult reproduction and survival depends on the intensity of intraspecific competition, a key environmental variable determining access to resources, in male Drosophila prolongata, a species with extended male-male contests. Contrary to expectations, more intense intraspecific competition partially mitigated the negative effects of the heatwave on male reproductive output. articles.title: Genomic signatures of recent human adaptation to the foraging-to-farming transition
articles.desc: Human populations across multiple regions transitioned from hunting and foraging to sedentary farming societies starting from ~10 thousand years ago (ka) to 12 ka, narrowing dietary diversity and transforming relationships with animals and pathogens. Here, to investigate how these ecological changes shaped human adaptations, we analysed high-coverage whole-genome sequence data from 1,092 individuals practising hunter-gatherer, agriculturalist and pastoralist lifestyles across 8 geographic regions spanning Africa, Asia and Oceania. Haplotype-based scans revealed pervasive recent positive selection on regulatory variation and genes associated with immune function across all subsistence modes, challenging the notion that agriculturalists alone experienced uniquely strong pathogenic pressures. By explicitly modelling correlations between allele frequencies and subsistence strategy, we uncovered convergent adaptations at a cross-continental scale in pathways beyond immunity, including metabolic, spermatogenesis and developmental pathways, supporting the life history hypothesis that energy allocation to growth, reproduction and maintenance shifted with the adoption of agriculture. Collectively, our findings illuminate the genetic legacy of ecological changes associated with the foraging-to-farming transition and highlight the central role of non-coding regulatory variation in human adaptation.

articles.title: Lynx reintroduction from a bottlenecked source exposes a lethal genetic defect
articles.desc: Conservation programmes worldwide use reintroductions and translocations as management tools to support endangered species. However, such efforts often result in small and isolated populations that face genetic challenges associated with reduced gene flow and inbreeding. Inbreeding depression is a well-known risk in such programmes, as increased homozygosity can expose recessive deleterious alleles, compromise fitness and threaten population persistence. Yet, no causal variant for a lethal disease has previously been identified in a wild population. Here we combine long-term health and population data with genomic analyses to identify a recessive loss-of-function allele causing lethal organ mineralization in young Eurasian lynx ( Lynx lynx ) from a reintroduced population in Switzerland. Spatio-temporal analyses revealed that the allele was introduced from one of the source populations and increased in frequency through founder effects and inbreeding. Our findings establish the first direct link between reintroduction history and a lethal genetic disease in the wild, illustrating how population genetic processes interact to shape the fate of a recessive deleterious allele and emphasize the vulnerability of small, isolated populations following reintroduction.
